statement: Lecture 1 agenda: caching at different levels, scaling, delegation, concurrency, communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda - Caching at different levels - Scaling - Delegation - Concurrency - Communication

statement: Caching can be done at several different levels of the architecture, not only in a central cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Caching at different levels

statement: Level 1: cache in the main memory of the API server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1. Main mem of API server

statement: API-server in-memory cache is limited in size.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ↳ limited

statement: If the API server goes down, its in-memory cached data is lost.
detail: Board word after 'server' reads 'cache'; audio context (student: 'if the application goes down, the cache is gone') suggests the meaning is server crash -> data lost. Likely also in audio around 00:10:03.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ↳ API server cache / data down
flags: check: board word may be 'crash' written as 'cache'

statement: With multiple API servers each holding a local in-memory cache, users can see inconsistent data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ↳ inconsistency

statement: Diagram: user to two API servers, each with its own local cache dot, both talking to one DB; a centralized remote cache (Redis) sits alongside.
detail: Label next to the cache shape is cut off at the page edge after 'Rem'; audio says 'centralized remote cache, which is say Redis'. Likely also in audio around 00:09:25.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis Rem c… (cut off at page edge)

statement: Level 2: database views, specifically materialized views, act as a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 2. DB views (materalized)

statement: Level 3: the browser's local storage can be used as a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 3. Brower (local sterage)

statement: Personalized recommendations (ranking) can be stored on the browser so the backend need not recompute them each visit.
detail: Small 'Recom ?' annotation above. Proposed by a student, endorsed by teacher as an excellent hack. Likely also in audio around 00:23:57.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Personalized Recom ( Ranking stored on Browser )

statement: Level 4: a CDN can cache API responses, not just static assets.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 4. CDN (cache response)

statement: Diagram: user → CDN → API server → DB; an endpoint like https://search…/popular can be served directly from the CDN.
detail: Host name on board is an unreadable squiggle; audio gives 'search.abc.com/popular'. Likely also in audio around 00:27:04.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: https// s~ . — /popular

statement: Level 5: the local disk of the API server can be used as a cache (emphasised with '!!').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 5. Disk of API serve !!

statement: Level 6: the load balancer / API gateway is also a place to cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 6. Load Balan (API GW

statement: Scaling is the ability to handle a large number of concurrent requests.
detail: 'concurrent' highlighted on the board. Likely also in audio around 00:35:18.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Ability to handle large number of concurrent requests

statement: There are two scaling strategies: vertical scaling and horizontal scaling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Two scaling strategies

statement: Vertical scaling is 'Hulk': make the infrastructure bulky by adding more CPU, RAM, disk.
detail: Hulk label is board-only per transcript search. Not found in transcript search; likely board-only.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Vertical scaling ——— Hulk ... Make infra bulky add more CPU, RAM, Disk

statement: Vertical scaling pro: easy to manage. Con: risk of downtime.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Eazy to manage / Risk of downtime

statement: Horizontal scaling is 'Minions': add more machines.
detail: Not found in transcript search; likely board-only.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Horizontal scaling ——— Minions ... Add more machines

statement: Horizontal scaling pros: linear amplification and fault tolerance. Cons: complex architecture and network partitioning.
detail: 'Fault Tolerance' and 'Network Partitioning' not found in transcript search; may be board-only. Likely also in audio around 00:40:47.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Linear amplification / Fault Tolerance / Complex Architecture / Network Partitioning

statement: A good general scaling plan: scale vertically first, then horizontally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Good scaling plan [in general] ... Scale Vertically ... Then horizontally

statement: No premature optimizations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No pre-mature optimizations

statement: For medium.com, scale vertically first, then horizontally (LB in front of multiple API servers).
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For our medium.com, we scale - vertically first - then horizontally

statement: Horizontal scaling gives near-infinite scale for API servers, but there is a catch: the stateful components (DB, cache) must handle that many concurrent requests.
detail: Boxed text on board reads literally 'can handle'; the catch is whether they can. Likely also in audio around 00:46:41.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Horizontal scaling ≈ ∞ scale , but there is a catch !! / Your stateful components like DB and cache can handle those many concurrent requests

statement: Whenever you scale, do it bottom up: scale the DB first, then the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hence whenever you scale , always do it bottom up ! ... Scale DB first ... Then API servers

statement: Three ways to scale a database: vertical scaling, read replicas, sharding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Scaling DB: vertical scaling / Read Replicas / Sharding

statement: Read replicas diagram: API server connects to both master and replica; master replicates to replica.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Read Replicas

statement: Sharding diagram: API server routes to three separate DB shards.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Sharding

statement: Adding basic analytics to the blog: the profile shows a count of blogs of a user (e.g. '74 essays').
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's add basic analytics to our blog ... 74 essays ... #blogs of a user

statement: What does not need to be done in realtime should not be done in realtime - the mantra for performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What does not need to be done in realtime should not be done in realtime

statement: Core idea of delegation: delegate and respond.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Core idea: Delegate & respond

statement: Delegation flow: (1) client calls API, (2) API puts a task on a broker, (3) API responds to client; workers consume from the broker and update the DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ① ... ② Task ... Broker ... worker ... update DB ... ③

statement: Store total_blogs pre-computed in the users table (id, name, bio, total_blogs) to avoid joins and runtime computation - a crude example.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Storing it pre-computed to avoid joins & runtime computation / * a crude example

statement: On publish, the API emits an ON_PUBLISH event to SQS; workers consume it and do total_blogs++ in the database.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ON_PUBLISH ... SQS ... total_blogs ++

statement: Similarly an ON-DELETE event is published and consumed to do total_blogs--.
detail: ON-DELETE not found in transcript search. Not found in transcript search; likely board-only.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Similarly, we publish and consume ON-DELETE event ↓ total_blogs --

statement: To index blogs on Elasticsearch, one could simply add business logic to the existing worker to also index on Elasticsearch.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we can simply - add business logic to worker & index blogs on elasticsearch

statement: Having the same worker do total_blogs++ and index on ES is not a good design: no separation of concerns; it looks like work for two separate teams.
detail: 'separation of concern' not found in transcript; board-only phrasing. Likely also in audio around 01:17:41.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: worker doing total_blogs++ & index on ES ... No separation of concern ... Seems something two separate teams should be working on !

statement: Hence use Kafka: the same event is consumed by two types of consumers (Search Service workers → ElasticSearch; Counter Service workers → Database).
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hence, we use Kafka / Same event consumed by two types of consumers

statement: Tasks that are delegated: long running tasks (spin up EC2 / video encoding), heavy computation query, batch & write, anything that could be eventual.
detail: Shown only briefly while scrolling; not found in transcript search. Not found in transcript search; likely board-only.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Tasks that are delegated - long running tasks ( spin up EC2 / video encoding ) - heavy computation query - batch & write - anything that could be eventual

statement: A broker is a buffer to keep the tasks and messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Brokers ... Buffer to keep the tasks & messages

statement: Two common broker implementations: message queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) and message streams (Kafka, Kinesis).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Two common implementations / Message Queues SQS, RabbitMQ / Message Streams Kafka, Kinesis

statement: In a message queue each message goes to one of the consumers; in a message stream every consumer type (e.g. Search, Analytics) reads the same messages at its own position.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Consumer / Consumer / Consumer ... Search ... Analytics

statement: Kafka is a message stream that holds the messages; internally it has topics, and every topic has n partitions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka is a message stream that holds the messages / Internally kafka has topic / Every topic has 'n' partitions

statement: A message is sent to a topic and, depending on the configured hash key, it is put into a partition.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Message is sent to a topic and depending on the configured hash key it is put into a partition

statement: The Kafka topic in the Medium example is named ON-PUBLISH.
detail: Resolves ASR 'unpublished' in F051/F052. Likely also in audio around 01:21:28.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ON-PUBLISH

statement: Within a partition messages are ordered; there is no ordering guarantee across partitions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Within partition, messages are ordered ↳ no ordering guarantee across partitions

statement: Limitation of Kafka: number of consumers (in a group) = number of partitions; with 3 partitions only 3 search consumers get messages, extra consumers get none.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: limitation of kafka / # consumers = # partitions / #partitions = 3 / No messages would be sent to them

statement: Concurrency is used to get faster execution, via threads or multiprocessing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Concurrency → to get faster execution → Threads / Multiprocessing

statement: Issues with concurrency: communication between threads, and concurrent use of shared resources (database, in-memory variables).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: communication b/w threads / concurrent use of shared resources → database / in-memory variables

statement: Handling concurrency: locks (optimistic & pessimistic), mutexes and semaphores, or going lock-free (CRDT).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Locks (optimistic & pessimistics) / Mutexes and semaphores / Go lock-free ^CRDT

statement: Locking will be covered in depth next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * we touch locking in depth the next week

statement: Concurrency in the blogging platform: if two users clap the same blog, the count must go up by 2.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Two users clap the same blog , count should be += 2

statement: Data is protected through transactions and atomic instructions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We protect our data through → Transactions → Atomic instructions

statement: Usual communication: client sends REQ, server does the heavy lifting and returns RES; the connection is kept open with a timeout.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: REQ / RES / Kept open with Timeout / Heavy lifting

statement: Short polling: the client calls the server every few seconds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Short Polling ... every few seconds

statement: Short polling examples: continuously refreshing a cricket score; checking if a server is ready.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: eg: continuously → refreshing cricket score → checking if server is ready

statement: Short polling disadvantages: HTTP overhead; lots of requests and responses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Disadvantages: → HTTP overhead → requests and responses

statement: Long polling: the server responds only when data is available; the connection is re-established after timeout and retried.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: only when data is available / Connection re-established after timeout & retried

statement: Long polling example: respond only when the ball is bowled.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: eg: response only when the ball is bowled

statement: Short polling sends a response right away; long polling sends a response only when done, keeping the connection open for the entire duration.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: short polling sends response right away / long polling sends response only when done - connection kept open for the entire duration

statement: EC2 provisioning: short polling gets status every few seconds; long polling gets a response when the server is ready.
detail: 'EC2 provisioning' not found in transcript search. Not found in transcript search; likely board-only.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: eg: EC2 provisioning ↳ short polling - gets status every few seconds ↳ long polling - gets response when server ready

statement: WebSockets: a bidirectional channel kept open between client and server; the server can proactively send data to the client.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Bidirectional Channel / Kept open / * Server can proactively send data to the client *

statement: Socket.IO is named next to WebSockets.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Socket.IO

statement: WebSocket advantages: realtime data transfer, low communication overhead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Advantages : - realtime data transfer - low communication overhead

statement: WebSocket applications: realtime communication, stock market ticker, live experiences, multiplayer games.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: realtime communication / stock market ticker / live experiences / multi player games

statement: Server-sent events: the server proactively sends data to the client; unidirectional.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Server-sent events / proactively sends data to client / Unidirectional

statement: SSE applications: stock market ticker, deployment logs streaming.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Applications: - stock market ticker - deployment logs streaming

statement: Communication in our blog: user ↔ API server over HTTP; API server ↔ database over persistent TCP; user ↔ Realtime likes service over WebSocket.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: HTTP / persistent TCP / WS / Realtime likes

statement: Realtime interactions: Twitter like count updates without refresh; on Medium when one article is clapped other readers should see it in realtime; Instagram live interaction.
case_study: Medium (medium.com) is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: on twitter, like count updates without refresh / on medium, one article clapped, other readers should see it in realtime / Instagram live interaction
